paragraphs: The Sovereign has no force except the legislative power, so it acts only through the laws. The laws are solely the authentic acts of the general will, so the Sovereign can act only when the people is assembled. The people in assembly, I shall be told, is a mere fantasy. Today it is; but two thousand years ago it was not. Has the nature of man changed?

The limits of what is possible in moral matters are less narrow than we imagine: it is our weaknesses, our vices and our prejudices that confine them. Base souls do not believe in great men; vile slaves smile mockingly at the name of liberty.

Let us judge what can be done by looking at what has been done. I shall say nothing of the Republics of ancient Greece; but the Roman Republic was, in my opinion, a great State, and Rome a great city. The last census counted four hundred thousand citizens in Rome who could bear arms, and the last count of the Empire’s population showed over four million citizens, leaving out subjects, foreigners, women, children and slaves.

What difficulties might one not imagine standing in the way of frequently assembling the vast population of this capital and its surroundings! Yet few weeks passed without the Roman people being assembled, and often several times. It exercised not only the rights of Sovereignty but also some of those of government. It dealt with certain matters and judged certain cases, and this whole people was found in the public meeting place almost as often as magistrates as it was as citizens.

If we went back to the earliest history of nations, we would find that most ancient governments, even monarchies such as the Macedonian and the Frankish, held similar councils. In any case, the one undeniable fact I have given answers every objection; to reason from what has actually happened to what is possible is sound logic.
